contributions.headingText: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome (RTS) is an autosomal recessive genodermatosis and cancer predisposition disorder, with a diagnostic hallmark of poikiloderma. Germline pathogenic sequence variants in the RECQL4 gene are present in about two thirds of patients and associated with RTS type 2, while variants in ANAPC1 are associated with RTS type 1.

618625 Rothmund–Thomson syndrome, type 1; RTS1

268400 Rothmund–Thomson syndrome, type 2; RTS2
LD2B Syndromes with premature ageing appearance as a major feature
Acceptable: poikiloderma congenitale; poikiloderma atrophicans and cataract.

Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type 1 (ANAPC1 variants in a subset, notably intronic splice variants, absence of RECQL4 variants, absence of osteosarcoma); Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type 2 (RECQL4 variants, osteosarcoma predisposition)

Skin and appendages: rash and pigmentation changes as discussed below, hyperkeratosis, sparse hair, skin cancers

Bone: skeletal abnormalities, osteosarcoma (associated with RTS type 2)

Eye: juvenile cataracts (associated with RTS type 1)

Constitution: small stature

The dermatological hallmark of RTS is an erythematous rash that starts on the cheeks in infancy and then spreads to the extremities, typically with truncal and abdominal sparing (see #38635Box 5.03). The rash enters a chronic lifelong phase with reticulated hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation, telangiectasia, and atrophy (collectively, poikiloderma) {20113479;20301415;11471165;16271439}. Poikiloderma is a hallmark of RTS, and all patients with RTS have some form of this skin finding. If the rash follows the classic pattern, consisting of an acute phase that starts in infancy and progresses to a chronic phase [[Wang LL, Levy ML. Chapter 140: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome, Bloom syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, Fanconi anaemia and poikiloderma with neutropenia. In: Hoeger P, Kinsler V, Yan A, et al., editors. Harper’s textbook of pediatric dermatology. 4th ed. Hoboken (NJ): John Wiley & Sons; 2020. pp. 1786–801. Bookref]], then a diagnosis of RTS is highly likely. If the rash is atypical either in pattern of spread or appearance, then two additional features of RTS are needed to make a diagnosis of probable RTS, including sparse scalp hair, eyelashes, or eyebrows; short stature; gastrointestinal disturbance (feeding problems, emesis, diarrhoea); radial ray defects; radiological bone abnormalities (radial ray and ulnar defects, absent or hypoplastic patella, osteopenia, abnormal trabeculation); dental abnormalities; nail abnormalities; hyperkeratosis; cataracts; and cancer including basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma and osteosarcoma {11471165;20301415}. Additional details on diagnostic criteria may be found in the RTS entry on the GeneReviews site {20301415}.

Additional findings include fused or missing bones, osteoporosis, brachymesophalangy {28486640}, and cataracts. RTS is also associated with an increased risk of malignancy in RTS type 2 patients. The most commonly associated cancers are osteosarcoma in childhood (~45% of patients with RTS type 2) {12734318} and squamous or basal cell carcinoma of the skin later in life {26892653}. Melanoma, while rare in RTS, has been reported {18347307}. Other less common cancers that may occur in later adulthood include lymphoma, adenocarcinoma of the gastrointestinal system, and squamous cell carcinoma of the head-and-neck region {10209473}. In the absence of death from cancer, patients appear to have a normal lifespan, although further natural history studies are needed {20301415}. Patients with RTS type 1 more commonly show juvenile cataracts as well as poikiloderma and sparse hair, eyebrows, or eyelashes, but do not have increased risk of osteosarcoma {31303264}.
RTS is a rare disorder with approximately 300 cases reported worldwide affecting all ethnic and racial groups {20113479;20301415;11471165;12734318}.

Pathogenic variants in the RECQL4 gene (8q24.3) are present in about two thirds of patients, designated as having RTS type 2 {12734318}, which is associated with an increased risk of osteosarcoma and other bone abnormalities {18647888}. Most of these are nonsense or frameshift variants and occur within the helicase domain, and less frequently within the N-terminus and C-terminus of the protein {20113479}.

Patients with RTS type 1 lack RECQL4 pathogenic variants; this form is more commonly associated with bilateral juvenile cataracts. A subset of RTS type 1 is due to mutation of ANAPC1, encoding the APC1 protein, a component of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) {31303264;20301415}.

RECQL4 is a member of the highly conserved RECQ DNA helicase family that shares sequence homology in the helicase domain. RECQ helicases are able to unwind duplex DNA to provide single-stranded templates for basic cellular processes such as replication, repair, recombination, and transcription {24606147}. RECQL4 is a multifunctional protein that has been implicated in several processes, including DNA replication, DNA damage repair, and maintenance of telomeres and of mitochondrial DNA integrity {19657341;29080750}. Pathogenic variants in RECQL4 have also been identified in patients with RAPADILINO syndrome (radial ray malformations, patella and palate abnormalities, diarrhoea and dislocated joints, limb abnormalities and little size, slender nose, and normal intelligence) {18716613} and Baller–Gerold syndrome {20301383}, both of which have clinical features overlapping those of RTS.

APC1 is a component of APC/C, which is an E3 ubiquitin ligase important for cell-cycle transition. Molecular studies have shown that the intron splice mutation of ANAPC1 found in RTS type 1 results in a 95 bp pseudoexon, causing nonsense-mediated decay of APC1 {31303264}. Both APC1 and RECQL4 proteins are involved in DNA replication and repair.

Patients with RTS type 2 are at increased risk of developing osteosarcoma (mean age 11 years) {17264332}, as well as basal cell and squamous carcinomas (mean age 34 years), at an earlier age than in the general population {18346259;12220274}. Reported sites of RTS osteosarcoma are distal femur (50%), proximal tibia (25%), proximal humerus (25%), distal fibula (7%), distal ulna (7%), distal radius (7%), and patella (7%) {17264332}.

Routine skin biopsies from individuals with RTS demonstrate characteristic histological features of poikiloderma, which can include hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, intraepidermal dyskeratotic cells, basal cell vacuolization, melanin incontinence, and prominent superficial dermal vessels [[Wang LL, Levy ML. Chapter 140: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome, Bloom syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, Fanconi anaemia and poikiloderma with neutropenia. In: Hoeger P, Kinsler V, Yan A, et al., editors. Harper’s textbook of pediatric dermatology. 4th ed. Hoboken (NJ): John Wiley & Sons; 2020. pp. 1786–801. Bookref]].

Histological subtypes of osteosarcoma in patients with RTS include osteoblastic (72%), fibroblastic (14%), chondroblastic (7%), and telangiectatic / giant cell–rich (7%). After chemotherapy, a good histological response of > 90% tumour necrosis occurs in 45% of patients, similar to what is seen in sporadic osteosarcomas {17264332}. Most cases of skin cancer are squamous cell or basal cell carcinomas {18346259}. However, there is one reported case of an amelanotic melanoma {18347307}.

A definitive diagnosis of RTS type 2 can be made by molecular testing for biallelic pathogenic variants in the RECQL4 gene. In approximately 40% of individuals with a clinical diagnosis of RTS, molecular genetic testing fails to identify a pathogenic variant in RECQL4. These individuals are designated as having RTS type 1. A proportion of probands with RTS type 1 will have pathogenic variants in the ANAPC1 gene (seven of nine families tested in one study {31303264}). Therefore, a lack of pathogenic variants does not rule out a diagnosis of RTS, as there remain RTS type 1 patients (~30% of all RTS) who lack both RECQL4 and ANAPC1 variants. The existence of one or more additional causative genes for RTS type 1 is likely {12734318;31303264;20301415}. Additional information on genetic testing was reviewed by Wang and Plon {20301415} and is present on the Genetic Testing Registry website of the US National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Essential: the diagnosis of RTS is established in a proband with the classic rash of RTS with onset, spread, and appearance described (see #38635Box 5.03); AND/OR biallelic pathogenic variants in ANAPC1 or RECQL4 identified on molecular genetic testing.

Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) / American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging is applicable to individual malignant tumours.

Patients with RTS type 2 (i.e. with RECQL4 pathogenic variants) are at increased risk of developing osteosarcoma {12734318} and of having bone defects {18647888}, and therefore must be counselled and followed closely. Some patients who develop osteosarcoma may have increased chemotherapy toxicity, and this should be anticipated and monitored closely during treatment {17264332}. To date, osteosarcoma and other malignant cancers are not thought to be associated with RTS type 1. Patients should have regular eye and skin examinations to check for cataracts and skin cancer, respectively.
